## Evaluation of $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\cos x}{1+x^2}\,dx$

**Setup.** Consider the complex function
$$f(z)=\frac{e^{iz}}{1+z^2}=\frac{e^{iz}}{(z-i)(z+i)}.$$
It is meromorphic with simple poles at $z=i$ and $z=-i$. We integrate $f$ over the closed contour $C_R$ consisting of the real segment $[-R,R]$ together with the upper semicircle $\Gamma_R=\{Re^{i\theta}:0\le\theta\le\pi\}$, for $R>1$.

**Residue.** The only pole inside $C_R$ is $z=i$. The residue there is
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=i}f(z)=\lim_{z\to i}(z-i)\frac{e^{iz}}{(z-i)(z+i)}=\frac{e^{i\cdot i}}{2i}=\frac{e^{-1}}{2i}=\frac{1}{2ie}.$$

By the residue theorem,
$$\oint_{C_R}f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\cdot\frac{1}{2ie}=\frac{\pi}{e}.$$

**Arc estimate.** On $\Gamma_R$, write $z=Re^{i\theta}=R(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$ with $\theta\in[0,\pi]$. Then
$$|e^{iz}|=e^{-R\sin\theta}\le 1 \quad(\text{since }\sin\theta\ge 0\text{ on }[0,\pi]),$$
and more sharply, by Jordan's lemma (since $1+z^2$ has degree $2$ and $e^{iz}$ decays in the upper half-plane),
$$\left|\int_{\Gamma_R}\frac{e^{iz}}{1+z^2}\,dz\right|\le \int_0^\pi \frac{e^{-R\sin\theta}}{R^2-1}R\,d\theta \le \frac{R}{R^2-1}\cdot\pi\;\xrightarrow[R\to\infty]{}\;0.$$
(Concretely, $|1+z^2|\ge R^2-1$ on $\Gamma_R$, and $\int_0^\pi e^{-R\sin\theta}d\theta\le\pi$.)

**Taking the limit.** Splitting the contour integral,
$$\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{e^{ix}}{1+x^2}\,dx+\int_{\Gamma_R}f(z)\,dz=\frac{\pi}{e}.$$
Letting $R\to\infty$, the arc term vanishes, so
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{1+x^2}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{e}.$$

**Extracting the cosine integral.** Taking real parts,
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\cos x}{1+x^2}\,dx=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\frac{\pi}{e}\right)=\frac{\pi}{e}.$$

(The imaginary part gives $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\sin x}{1+x^2}\,dx=0$, consistent with the integrand being odd.)

$$\boxed{\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\cos x}{1+x^2}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{e}}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
